episodes.title: How Fold Mountains Form
sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 4 (Distribution of Oceans and Continents): India collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago causing rapid uplift of the Himalayas; the process is still continuing
NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 5 (Geomorphic Processes): orogeny is mountain building through severe folding; upfolds are anticlines and downfolds synclines
NCERT Class 11, India: Physical Environment, ch. 2: the Himalayas are a series of parallel ranges with faults, folds and thrust planes

USGS, This Dynamic Earth, 'The Himalayas: Two continents collide': Tethys Sea between India and Asia; India moved north after Pangaea broke up about 200 million years ago; similar rock density so neither plate subducted; Himalayas rise more than 1 cm a year; Tethys fossils in Tibetan sandstones

quiz.q: Why did the crust crumple upward when India met Asia?
options: One plate sank quickly under the other
Both plates were too light to sink, so the crust was pushed up
A volcano erupted under the sea
quiz.why: Both continental plates have about the same density, so neither sank and the crust rose.

quiz.q: What is a syncline?
quiz.why: Upfolds are anticlines; downfolds are synclines.

quiz.q: Roughly when did India collide with Asia?
quiz.why: NCERT and USGS both give about 40 to 50 million years ago.

review.note: Facts were read against NCERT Class 11 (Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 4 and 5; India: Physical Environment ch. 2) and the USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' page on the Himalayas. Diagrams are schematic, no map. The orbital photo is cropped to peaks; check that no place label shows. Moving facts: the uplift rate is an estimate and varies by study.

episodes.title: Ocean Currents in 60 Seconds
sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 13 (Movements of Ocean Water): definition of currents vs waves; primary forces (solar heating, wind, gravity, Coriolis); Coriolis turns water right in the north, left in the south, making large circular currents; surface currents about 10% of ocean water, deep currents 90%; cold currents on west coasts and warm on east coasts in low and middle latitudes; west coasts bordered by cool water have fog but are arid; west coasts in middle and higher latitudes bordered by warm water have a marine climate; best fishing grounds in mixing zones
NOAA Ocean Service, 'What is the global ocean conveyor belt?': deep circulation driven by temperature and salinity

quiz.q: In the northern hemisphere, the Coriolis force turns moving water to the…
quiz.why: Right in the northern hemisphere, left in the southern.

quiz.q: About what share of ocean water moves in surface currents?
quiz.why: Surface currents hold about a tenth; deep currents hold the other nine-tenths.

quiz.q: Where are the world's best fishing grounds usually found?
options: In the middle of warm currents
Where warm and cold currents mix
quiz.why: The video ends on the mixing zones of warm and cold currents.

review.note: Facts were read against NCERT Class 11 Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 13 and NOAA Ocean Service's conveyor-belt page. The NASA flow visualisation shows coastlines but no national borders; crop to open ocean and check before publishing. Moving facts: none known.

episodes.title: Tropical and Temperate Cyclones
sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 9 (Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems): conditions for tropical cyclones (sea above 27°C, Coriolis force, small variation in vertical wind speed, pre-existing low, upper divergence); eye and eye wall; landfall; tropical cyclones dissipate on reaching land; extra-tropical cyclones form along the polar front with warm and cold fronts, cover a larger area, move west to east; tropical cyclones originate only over seas, have higher wind velocity, move east to west

quiz.q: Which sea-surface temperature does NCERT give for tropical cyclones to form?
quiz.why: A large sea surface warmer than 27°C is the first condition.

quiz.q: Which cyclones have clear warm and cold fronts?
quiz.why: Temperate cyclones form along the polar front, with warm and cold fronts.

quiz.q: What is the calm centre of a tropical cyclone called?
quiz.why: The eye is a calm region of sinking air; the eye wall surrounds it.

review.note: Facts were read against NCERT Class 11 Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 9. Satellite pictures are over open ocean with no labels; check that no coastline or border line is drawn. Moving facts: none known.

episodes.title: How a Tsunami Crosses an Ocean
sources: NOAA/NWS Tsunami.gov FAQ: in the deep ocean tsunamis can move over 500 mph, like a jet plane, and cross oceans in less than a day; wavelength 60–300 miles; deep-ocean waves rarely more than three feet high

NCERT Class 11, India: Physical Environment, ch. 6 (Natural Hazards and Disasters): tsunamis caused by sudden sea-floor movement from earthquakes and volcanic eruptions; a ship rises only a metre or two and each rise and fall takes several minutes; in shallow water wavelength reduces and height increases; India joined the International Tsunami Warning System after the December 2004 tsunami
INCOIS (Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Ministry of Earth Sciences) is in Hyderabad and runs India's tsunami early warning (Wikipedia summary of INCOIS)

quiz.q: How fast can a tsunami travel in the deep ocean?
options: It does not move until it reaches land
quiz.why: Over 500 mph (about 800 km/h) in deep water.

quiz.q: What happens to a tsunami as it enters shallow water?
options: It slows down and grows taller
quiz.why: Shallow water shortens the wave and raises its height.

quiz.q: Which institution issues India's tsunami warnings?
quiz.why: India's tsunami early warning comes from INCOIS in Hyderabad.

review.note: Tone SERIOUS: the video names the 2004 tsunami but is about how the wave travels; it gives no death toll and shows no damage. Facts were read against NOAA's Tsunami.gov FAQ and NCERT Class 11 India: Physical Environment ch. 6. INCOIS's own portal page did not load from this computer; its role was checked on a summary page, so confirm on incois.gov.in before approval. On screen, 500 mph is shown as about 800 km/h and 60–300 miles as about 100–500 km. A NOAA tsunami-energy map was considered and left out (world map). Moving facts: none known.

episodes.title: Barren Island: India's Live Volcano
sources: Wikipedia, 'Barren Island (Andaman Islands)' (which cites the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and the Geological Survey of India): only confirmed active volcano in the Indian subcontinent and the only active one on the Sumatra–Myanmar chain; about 138 km north-east of Port Blair; first recorded eruption 1787, further eruptions in 1789, 1795, 1803–04 and 1852; nearly a century and a half of dormancy; 1991 eruption lasting six months; eruptions 2017–2019
Commons file pages for the 1789 and 1885 illustrations (dates and makers of the drawings)

quiz.q: In which sea does Barren Island lie?
quiz.why: It is in the Andaman Sea, about 138 km from Port Blair.

quiz.q: When was Barren Island's first recorded eruption?
quiz.why: The record begins in 1787.

quiz.q: What makes Barren Island special?
options: It is India's only confirmed active volcano
quiz.why: The video calls it India's only confirmed active volcano.

review.note: Facts were read against the Wikipedia article on Barren Island, which cites the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and GSI. The GVP page itself showed a verification wall to this computer, so check the eruption list on volcano.si.edu (vn=260010) before approval. Moving facts: eruptions continue (the summary lists one in 2025), so the script says 'repeated eruptions in our own time' rather than a latest date.

episodes.title: Why Himalayan Slopes Slide
sources: NCERT Class 11, India: Physical Environment, ch. 6 (Natural Hazards and Disasters): landslide defined as rapid downslope movement of rock and debris under gravity, failing along a shear plane; very high vulnerability zones are highly unstable, relatively young mountains in the Himalayas, high-rainfall steep slopes and quake-prone areas; mitigation by restricting roads, dams and large settlements in high-vulnerability zones, large-scale afforestation, bunds and terrace farming
NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 5 (Geomorphic Processes): mass movements carry rock debris downslope under gravity
NCERT Class 11, India: Physical Environment, ch. 6: indiscriminate deforestation and construction add to hazards

quiz.q: Which force moves the debris in a landslide?
quiz.why: Mass movements are driven by gravity.

quiz.q: Which of these does NCERT suggest to reduce landslides?
options: Building more roads on steep slopes
Building large settlements in high-risk zones
quiz.why: Afforestation, bunds and terraces help; building in high-risk zones should be restricted.

quiz.q: Why are the Himalayas so prone to landslides?
options: They are young, steep, unstable and quake-prone
They are very old and worn down
They are made only of hard granite
quiz.why: Young, steep, unstable rock that is shaken by earthquakes and soaked by rain.

review.note: Tone SERIOUS (a hazard; no victims are named or shown). Facts were read against NCERT Class 11 India: Physical Environment ch. 6 and Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 5. Check the road clip for readable faces or number plates. Moving facts: none known.

episodes.title: Glaciers and the Rivers They Feed
sources: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Retreat of the Gangotri Glacier': 30.2 km long, 0.5–2.5 km wide, one of the largest in the Himalaya; receding since 1780, faster after 1971; retreated more than 850 m over the last 25 years (to 2001)

NCERT Class 11, India: Physical Environment, ch. 3 (Drainage System): the Bhagirathi rises in the Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh (3,900 m); Himalayan rivers are perennial because they are fed by melting snow and precipitation

NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 6 (Landforms and their Evolution): glaciers move because of gravity, a few centimetres to a few metres a day; glacial erosion and deposition landforms

quiz.q: Which river is born at Gaumukh, the snout of the Gangotri glacier?
quiz.why: The Bhagirathi rises at Gaumukh; the Alaknanda rises at Satopanth glacier.

quiz.q: Why do Himalayan rivers flow all year?
options: They are fed by both snow melt and rain
They are fed only by groundwater
They are dammed at the source
It rains every day in the Himalayas
quiz.why: Snow melt plus rain makes them perennial.

quiz.q: What shape of valley does a glacier carve?
quiz.why: Glacial erosion widens valleys into a U shape.

review.note: Facts were read against NASA Earth Observatory's Gangotri page and NCERT Class 11 (India: Physical Environment ch. 3; Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 6). The U-shaped valley is standard NCERT glacial-landform content; confirm the wording in ch. 6 if needed. The NASA retreat image shows terminus lines but no borders. Moving facts: Gangotri's length and retreat figures are from NASA's 2001-era analysis; newer studies give other numbers.

episodes.title: How a River Leaves an Oxbow Lake
sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 6 (Landforms and their Evolution): streams on gentle slopes develop meandering courses; active deposition along the convex bank and undercutting along the concave bank; as meanders grow into deep loops they may get cut off by erosion at the inflection points and are left as ox-bow lakes; floodplains show natural levees and oxbow lakes; channels in plains leave cut-off courses that fill up gradually

quiz.q: On which bank of a meander does the river erode most?
quiz.why: Fast water undercuts the concave (outer) bank.

quiz.q: What finally creates an oxbow lake?
options: The river cutting across the narrow neck of a loop
quiz.why: The neck narrows until the river cuts across it and leaves the loop.

quiz.q: Where are oxbow lakes most common?
quiz.why: Meanders and oxbows form where the gradient is gentle, on floodplains.

review.note: Facts were read against NCERT Class 11 Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 6. Diagrams are schematic. Moving facts: none.

episodes.title: Urban Heat Islands
sources: US EPA, 'Learn About Heat Islands': urban areas about 1–7°F warmer by day and 2–5°F warmer at night than outlying areas (US studies); pavements and roofing absorb and emit more of the Sun's heat; trees, vegetation and water bodies cool through shade, transpiration and evaporation; human-generated waste heat adds to it
US EPA Heat Island Reduction Solutions pages: trees and vegetation, green roofs, cool roofs, cool pavements

quiz.q: What is an urban heat island?
options: An island city in the sea
A city area warmer than its surroundings
quiz.why: Cities are often warmer than the countryside around them.

quiz.q: Which of these cools a city?
quiz.why: Trees and water cool the air by shade, transpiration and evaporation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cause of heat islands?
options: Roads and roofs storing the Sun's heat
quiz.why: Built surfaces absorb more heat and release it after sunset.

review.note: Facts were read against the US EPA heat island pages. The temperature figures are from US studies and are labelled that way on screen; no Indian city figure is claimed. The bars diagram uses the top of each range. Moving facts: none known.

episodes.title: Wetlands: Nature's Kidneys
sources: US EPA, 'Why are Wetlands Important?': wetlands protect and improve water quality, act as natural sponges that trap and slowly release floodwater, maintain surface flow in dry periods, provide fish and wildlife habitat; Mississippi bottomland wetlands once stored at least 60 days of floodwater
Wikipedia, 'Ramsar Convention': signed at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 (World Wetlands Day)
Wikipedia, 'List of Ramsar sites in India': Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park were India's first sites, 1 October 1981

quiz.q: Why are wetlands called nature's kidneys?
quiz.why: Plants slow the flow and mud settles out, so the water moving on is cleaner.

quiz.q: Where was the Ramsar Convention signed?
quiz.why: Signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971.

quiz.q: Which two were India's first Ramsar sites?
quiz.why: Chilika and Keoladeo joined the list in 1981.

review.note: Facts were read against US EPA's wetlands page and summary pages for the Ramsar Convention and India's Ramsar list; check the 1981 date on the Ramsar Sites Information Service before approval. 'Nature's kidneys' is a common nickname, not an official term. Video 233 (Ramsar sites) covers the list itself, so this one stays on what wetlands do. Moving facts: India's Ramsar count changes often, so no count is given.
